quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Every Tuesday morning, the central market dims its lights and turns off its loudspeakers for an hour. The 'quiet hour' began after a shopper with sensory sensitivities asked whether the noise could be reduced. Other customers soon noticed the difference: conversations were easier, children were calmer, and older shoppers found the hour less tiring. Stallholders say sales during the quiet hour are as good as at any other time, and two neighboring markets have started copying the idea.
options: A Quiet Hour Many Shoppers Welcome
Dimmed Lights and Silent Loudspeakers
How One Request Started a Market Tradition
Making Public Spaces More Comfortable
quests.correctAnswer: A Quiet Hour Many Shoppers Welcome
quests.hint: One shopper began it, but ask who benefits in the end.
quests.explanation: Comfortable public spaces is too broad, and the lights and speakers describe only how the hour works. The origin story is just the beginning; the passage stresses that many different shoppers gain.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title covers the quiet hour and the range of people it helps, without stretching to all public spaces.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Until two years ago, buses in the city stopped at midnight, leaving nurses, cleaners, and kitchen staff to walk or pay for taxis after late shifts. The council's new night routes run every thirty minutes along the busiest corridors and cost the same as daytime fares. Ridership has exceeded forecasts, and hospital managers say staff arrive less tired. However, some routes still miss neighborhoods where many shift workers live, and residents are asking for extensions.
options: Hospital Staff Arriving Less Tired
Improving Public Transport in Cities
Half-Hourly Buses Along Busy Corridors
Progress and Gaps in Night Buses for Shift Workers
quests.correctAnswer: Progress and Gaps in Night Buses for Shift Workers
quests.hint: The word 'however' introduces something that a good title should not leave out.
quests.explanation: Improving public transport in general is far too wide, and the half-hourly buses and the less tired staff are single details of the service or its results. The passage reports the improvement and the remaining shortfall together.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice combines the benefits of the night routes with the unresolved gaps the passage ends on.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: The oak in the schoolyard is older than the school, the town hall, and probably the town's name. When engineers proposed felling it to widen the entrance, students collected leaves, measured its trunk, and wrote to the council. Their evidence showed that the tree shaded three classrooms, sheltered nesting birds, and was one of the few in the district that had survived the last storm. The entrance was redesigned around it, and the tree now appears on the school badge.
options: Redesigning a School Entrance Around a Tree
Students Save a Schoolyard Oak
Measuring the Trunk of an Old Oak
Protecting Old Trees in Towns and Cities
quests.correctAnswer: Students Save a Schoolyard Oak
quests.hint: Which title includes who acted, what they did, and what it achieved?
quests.explanation: Protecting old trees is a general topic, measuring is one action, and the entrance redesign is only the outcome. The passage tells how the students' evidence saved the tree.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title shows the students, their method, and the tree's survival in one title.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Regional airports rarely make a profit, and yet many governments continue to fund them. The reasoning is that a small runway connects a remote island to hospitals, gives local businesses access to customers, and provides an evacuation route in emergencies. Critics counter that the same money could improve ferries or roads. The debate rarely ends in a clear winner because the airport's value is measured not in tickets sold but in the lifeline it provides.
options: The Cost of Modern Air Travel
Weighing the Value of Loss-Making Regional Airports
Critics Who Prefer Better Roads
Evacuation Routes for Island Residents
quests.correctAnswer: Weighing the Value of Loss-Making Regional Airports
quests.hint: Notice that the passage gives both a defense and an objection.
quests.explanation: The title about the cost of air travel changes the subject, and the evacuation-route and better-roads titles each pick one side or one benefit. The passage is a balanced discussion of whether these airports are worth funding.
quests.whyThisTitle: It reflects the debate between the airports' public value and their financial losses.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Some cities are now mapping sound the way they map traffic. Volunteers carry small microphones on their commutes, and the recordings are combined into a picture of the loudest and quietest streets. Officials use the maps to decide where to plant hedges, reduce speed limits, or reroute delivery trucks. The maps also reveal quiet corners that residents value but planners had overlooked, which are now being protected.
options: Rerouting Delivery Trucks Away from Homes
Volunteers Carrying Microphones on Commutes
The Effects of Noise on City Life
Using Sound Maps to Plan a Quieter City
quests.correctAnswer: Using Sound Maps to Plan a Quieter City
quests.hint: Ask what the maps are used for, not just how they are made.
quests.explanation: Noise effects are never discussed, and the microphones and truck rerouting are single elements. The passage covers making the maps and using them.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title joins the sound mapping with its use in city planning.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In the corridors of a children's hospital, paintings by local artists hang at a child's eye level. The program began when a nurse noticed that young patients often stared at blank ceilings while being wheeled to treatment. Now, an art volunteer visits each week to help children make their own pictures, which are displayed beside the professionals'. Staff say that children walk more willingly to appointments, and parents report that the corridors feel less frightening.
options: Paintings Hung at a Child's Eye Level
The Healing Power of the Arts
How Art Makes a Children's Hospital Less Frightening
A Nurse's Observation of Blank Ceilings
quests.correctAnswer: How Art Makes a Children's Hospital Less Frightening
quests.hint: Which title tells you what the art program achieves?
quests.explanation: The healing power of the arts is too general, and the eye-level paintings and the nurse's observation are only parts of the program's story. The passage is about the effect on the children's experience.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title ties the program's elements to the outcome staff and parents report.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Overnight sleeper trains, once thought obsolete, are being revived across Europe. Travelers who choose them save the cost of a hotel night and arrive in the center of a city rather than at a distant airport. Operators are adding private cabins and better bedding, and some routes now sell out weeks ahead. Still, the trains are slow and expensive to run, so their comeback depends on governments supporting them rather than on ticket sales alone.
options: Saving on a Night in a Hotel
Private Cabins with Better Bedding
The Return of Sleeper Trains and What It Depends On
The Future of Rail Travel
quests.correctAnswer: The Return of Sleeper Trains and What It Depends On
quests.hint: Notice that the last sentence sets a condition for the comeback. What is that condition?
quests.explanation: The future of rail travel is much wider, and cabins and hotel savings are individual points. The passage covers the revival and the condition attached to it.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice captures both the comeback and the support it requires.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Many adults assume they are too old to learn an instrument, yet community music schools report a growing number of students over sixty. Teachers say older learners bring patience and a willingness to practice slowly, though they can be harder on themselves than children. Progress may be gradual, but studies suggest that learning music can sharpen memory and give retirees a routine and new friends. The oldest student at one school began the cello at eighty-one.
options: Benefits of Learning Any New Skill
Discovering Music Later in Life
Older Learners Being Hard on Themselves
An Eighty-One-Year-Old Cello Beginner
quests.correctAnswer: Discovering Music Later in Life
quests.hint: Look at the group of people the passage is about, and what they gain.
quests.explanation: Any new skill goes beyond music, the cello student is one example, and self-criticism is a minor point. The passage concerns older adults taking up music and what they gain.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title reflects the growing group of adult learners and the benefits described.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: For decades, the river that runs through the city was hidden behind concrete walls and used as a drain. Officials have now removed sections of the walls, planted reeds along the banks, and reopened paths beside the water. Fish have returned, and so have walkers and cyclists. Some residents, however, are concerned that the newly attractive riverside will push up rents. The council says it is studying ways to keep the area affordable.
options: Improving Life Through Urban Green Spaces
Rising Rents Beside the River
Reviving a River and Raising New Worries
Removing Concrete Walls Along the Banks
quests.correctAnswer: Reviving a River and Raising New Worries
quests.hint: Which title covers both the improvement and the worry?
quests.explanation: Green spaces in general is too broad, and the walls and rents are each half of the story. The passage reports the river's revival and the concern that follows.
quests.whyThisTitle: It joins the river's restoration and the residents' concern in one title.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Delivery companies in crowded cities are replacing vans with electric cargo bikes. In dense streets, a bike can be quicker than a van that circles for parking, and it produces no exhaust. Riders can carry hundreds of kilos and reach pedestrian zones that vans cannot. The main limit is distance: bikes are ideal within a few kilometers of a depot but impractical for long routes, so most companies use both.
options: Where Cargo Bikes Beat Delivery Vans
Cleaner Cities: Reducing Pollution from Traffic
The Distance Limits of Electric Bikes
Carrying Hundreds of Kilos by Bike
quests.correctAnswer: Where Cargo Bikes Beat Delivery Vans
quests.hint: Decide what the passage says about when bikes are better and when they are not.
quests.explanation: Pollution is one possible benefit, the load capacity is one detail, and the distance limit is one drawback. The passage compares the situations where bikes do better than vans.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title covers the advantages in dense areas and the limits that keep vans in use.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Many teachers were once told that students are 'visual' or 'auditory' learners and should be taught accordingly. Experiments, however, have found little evidence that matching lessons to a preferred style improves results. What helps is using several methods for every topic, since seeing, hearing, and doing all strengthen memory in different ways. Teachers who dropped the labels and varied their lessons report that more students engage.
options: Engaging More Students in Class
Why Varied Teaching Works Better Than Learning Labels
Visual and Auditory Learners
How People Learn New Information
quests.correctAnswer: Why Varied Teaching Works Better Than Learning Labels
quests.hint: The passage challenges one idea and supports another. Which title reflects both?
quests.explanation: How people learn is too broad, the learner types are only the idea being challenged, and student engagement is one result. The passage argues for varied teaching in place of labeling.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title states the passage's conclusion and the idea it replaces.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Neatly mown lawns look tidy, but for insects they are deserts. Some homeowners now let patches of grass grow long and allow clover and dandelions to flower. Within a season, bees and butterflies appear, and the wild patch costs less to maintain than a manicured lawn. Neighbors sometimes complain about untidiness, so a growing number of councils give out signs explaining that the meadow is deliberate.
options: Signs Explaining Deliberate Meadows to Neighbors
Protecting Wildlife in Gardens
Saving Money on Lawn Care
Letting Lawns Grow Wild for Insects
quests.correctAnswer: Letting Lawns Grow Wild for Insects
quests.hint: Which title names the action the passage describes and the reason for it?
quests.explanation: Wildlife protection is broader, and the signs and savings are supporting details. The passage is about deliberately leaving lawn patches uncut to help insects.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice names the practice and the insect benefit that motivates it.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Tiny houses, often smaller than thirty square meters, appeal to people who want to spend less and own less. Bills shrink, and cleaning takes minutes. Yet living in so little space demands constant organization, and couples or people working from home report that privacy is hard to find. Many owners also face difficulty finding legal places to park or build. The lifestyle suits some people well, but it involves trade-offs that photographs rarely show.
options: Lower Bills in Small Homes
The Hidden Trade-Offs of Tiny Houses
Finding Legal Places to Park
How to Choose Where and How to Live in a City
quests.correctAnswer: The Hidden Trade-Offs of Tiny Houses
quests.hint: Look at how the final sentence sums up the whole passage. What is its main point?
quests.explanation: Choosing where and how to live is much too general, and the parking and lower-bills titles are one difficulty and one advantage. The passage weighs the benefits against the drawbacks.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title reflects the balance of appealing features and the less visible downsides.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Every winter, thousands of volunteers spend an hour counting the birds in their gardens and send the results to researchers. A single count is small, but together the numbers reveal which species are declining and which are recovering. Scientists say the data would take years and enormous funds to collect alone. Volunteers, for their part, often report that the hour changes how they see their own gardens.
options: How Bird Counts Help Scientists
Seeing Gardens in a New Way
Counting Birds for an Hour in Winter
The Role of Volunteers in Science
quests.correctAnswer: How Bird Counts Help Scientists
quests.hint: Which title covers who counts, what they achieve, and for whom?
quests.explanation: The role of volunteers in science is broader, and the hour of counting and the new view of gardens are single details. The passage explains what the counts contribute to research.
quests.whyThisTitle: It captures the volunteers' contribution to the scientists' work.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Many adults say they are 'bad at math' and mean it as a fact about themselves. Teachers who study math anxiety point out that the feeling often begins with a single embarrassing moment, such as being asked to solve a problem at the board. Worry then takes up mental space, making the next problem harder. Classes that let students work in pairs and allow mistakes without penalty show less anxiety and better results.
options: Solving Problems at the Board
Easing Math Anxiety in Class
Why Some Subjects Feel Difficult
Working in Pairs Without Penalty
quests.correctAnswer: Easing Math Anxiety in Class
quests.hint: Ask what problem the passage explains and what it offers to address it.
quests.explanation: Difficult subjects is too general, and the board and pairs are pieces of the explanation and solution. The passage links the anxiety's origins with a classroom response.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title joins the problem and the approaches that reduce it.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In a time bank, members exchange hours instead of money. One hour spent fixing a bicycle earns an hour of piano lessons from someone else. Everyone's time is valued equally, whether they are a retired engineer or a student. Members often find that they receive help they would never have paid for and give help they never knew they could. The scheme works best when it is easy to see what each person can offer.
options: How Time Banks Trade Skills
Alternatives to Using Money
Trading Bicycle Repair for Piano Lessons
Retired Engineers Helping Students
quests.correctAnswer: How Time Banks Trade Skills
quests.hint: Look at what members give and what they receive, and at what takes the place of payment in this system.
quests.explanation: Alternatives to money is too broad, and the swap and the engineers are examples. The passage describes the whole system of hour-for-hour exchange.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title explains the idea that equal hours of skill become a shared currency.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: It may seem strange to set a forest on fire on purpose. Yet in fire-prone regions, foresters carry out small, controlled burns during mild weather to clear dry undergrowth. By removing the fuel that would feed a large fire, they reduce the risk of a devastating one later. Many native plants even depend on periodic fire to release seeds. Communities near forests, however, need clear warnings, since smoke can disturb people with breathing difficulties.
options: Warnings About Smoke for Nearby Residents
Fire Helping Native Plants Release Seeds
Preventing Natural Disasters
Small Fires Set by Foresters
quests.correctAnswer: Small Fires Set by Foresters
quests.hint: The passage begins with a puzzle. Which title answers it in full?
quests.explanation: Preventing disasters is far wider, and the seeds and the warnings are secondary points. The core is that small fires reduce the risk of large ones.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice answers the question the opening raises with the main reason.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Fees for youth sports have risen steadily, and some families now choose between paying for equipment and paying for a season. Clubs say costs for pitches, insurance, and coaches keep growing. In response, some have introduced sliding fees, lending equipment, or asking local businesses to sponsor teams. Early results suggest that children who might have stopped playing are staying, though funding remains uncertain.
options: Keeping Youth Sports Affordable
Lending Equipment to Young Players
The Value of Children Playing Sports
Rising Costs for Pitches and Insurance
quests.correctAnswer: Keeping Youth Sports Affordable
quests.hint: Look for the problem, the responses, and the results.
quests.explanation: The value of sports is never argued, and lending equipment and rising costs are single points. The passage covers the cost problem and the measures to solve it.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title combines the affordability problem with the clubs' efforts to address it.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Ramps built beside curbs for wheelchair users turned out to help many others: parents with strollers, travelers with suitcases, delivery workers with carts. Designers call this the curb-cut effect, in which a feature made for one group becomes useful for all. Subtitles were first created for deaf viewers, yet many people now use them in noisy places or to follow accents. Designing carefully for a specific need can therefore widen a product's usefulness far beyond its intended audience.
options: Making Cities Accessible to Disabled People
Ramps Beside Street Curbs
Subtitles for Noisy Places
How Designing for One Helps All
quests.correctAnswer: How Designing for One Helps All
quests.hint: Two examples appear. What idea do they share?
quests.explanation: Accessible cities and the curb ramps cover one field, and the subtitles are one example. The final sentence states the general principle both examples illustrate.
quests.whyThisTitle: It expresses the principle that the two examples demonstrate.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A supermarket chain trialed home delivery for customers over seventy. Drivers were asked to carry bags to the kitchen, chat for a minute, and note if anything seemed wrong. Several times, they alerted families about a fall or confusion. The service was more expensive than standard delivery, but customers valued the checks, and some communities have asked to expand the scheme.
options: Carrying Bags into the Kitchen
The Higher Cost of a Special Service
Helping Older People Live Independently at Home
Deliveries That Also Check on Older Customers
quests.correctAnswer: Deliveries That Also Check on Older Customers
quests.hint: What does the service do beyond delivering groceries?
quests.explanation: Living independently is broader, and the bags and cost are single details. The trial's distinguishing feature is the added check on customers' wellbeing.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title joins the delivery with the safety checks that give the scheme its value.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A small lake was infested with an invasive weed that clogged propellers and crowded out native plants. Volunteers spent summers pulling it by hand, but it returned each year. Only when the lake association set up a cleaning station at the boat ramp did the spread slow. Boats had been carrying fragments of the weed from other lakes, and washing them before launch prevented new infestations.
options: Weeds Clogging Boat Propellers
Volunteers Pulling Weeds by Hand Each Summer
Stopping a Lake Weed at the Boat Ramp
Protecting Lakes from Pollution
quests.correctAnswer: Stopping a Lake Weed at the Boat Ramp
quests.hint: Which approach actually worked, and where was it applied?
quests.explanation: Pollution is a different topic, pulling by hand is the method that failed, and propeller clogging is a symptom. The passage centers on the measure that stopped the spread.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title names the effective solution and the place where it was applied.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Each summer, farms depend on seasonal workers to pick fruit that cannot be harvested by machine. Many workers travel from abroad, living in shared accommodation and working long days. Farmers say the fruit would rot without them, and workers value the wages, which can exceed what they earn at home. Advocates argue that housing and working conditions vary widely and that clearer standards would benefit both groups.
options: Farms and Seasonal Workers Needing Clearer Standards
Workers, Borders, and Global Labor
Living in Shared Accommodation
Wages Higher Than at Home
quests.correctAnswer: Farms and Seasonal Workers Needing Clearer Standards
quests.hint: Ask who depends on whom in this passage, and what the advocates ask for.
quests.explanation: Global labor movements are too wide, and the housing and wages are single details. The passage covers the mutual reliance and the call for clearer standards.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice combines both sides' dependence and the proposal in the final sentence.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Students often choose universities by ranking, assuming that the higher the ranking, the better the education. Researchers who follow graduates find that outcomes depend more on what students do than on where they study: whether they seek out teachers, join projects, and take on challenges. A student at a modest university who takes advantage of these opportunities can outperform a passive student at a famous one. Rankings measure many things, but rarely how engaged a student will be.
options: Why Engagement Beats Rankings
Joining Projects and Seeking Out Teachers
Choosing the Right University
How University Rankings Are Measured
quests.correctAnswer: Why Engagement Beats Rankings
quests.hint: The passage compares two things. Which one does it rate higher?
quests.explanation: Choosing a university is broader, and joining projects and measuring rankings are pieces of the comparison. The passage argues that engagement counts for more than ranking.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title reflects the comparison and the conclusion the researchers draw.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When cities added countdown timers to pedestrian signals, some feared that people would rush. In practice, studies found that walkers crossed at a steadier pace and fewer started when too little time remained. Drivers also benefited, since they could see when the light would change and avoid sudden braking. The timers cost little to install, and several cities plan to add them at all busy crossings.
options: Improving Road Safety in Cities
Walkers Crossing at a Steadier Pace
Why Crossing Timers Help Everyone
Fears About People Rushing
quests.correctAnswer: Why Crossing Timers Help Everyone
quests.hint: Which title covers both walkers and drivers?
quests.explanation: Road safety in cities is broader, the steadier pace is only the walkers' benefit, and the fear of rushing is the expectation the studies contradicted. The passage shows the timers' benefits for everyone at crossings.
quests.whyThisTitle: It captures the timers' effect on both walkers and drivers.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: A community theater invited local teenagers to build a play from their own stories. At first, the sessions were awkward, with more silence than speech. As the weeks passed, participants began to trust each other, and their scenes about school, family, and worry grew honest and funny. The performance drew a full house, and several teenagers said it was the first time adults had listened without correcting them.
options: Awkward Silences in the First Sessions
A Full House on Opening Night
Giving Teenagers a Voice Through Theater
Ways Communities Support Young People Through Art
quests.correctAnswer: Giving Teenagers a Voice Through Theater
quests.hint: Look at the final sentence. What did the teenagers gain?
quests.explanation: Community support is a general topic, and the silences and the full house are moments in the story. The passage's heart is that the teenagers were finally heard.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title reflects the outcome the teenagers describe: being listened to.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Homeowners often spend money on new windows or solar panels while ignoring the attic. Yet heat rises, and a poorly insulated roof can account for a quarter of a home's heat loss. Adding insulation is among the cheapest improvements and pays for itself within a few winters. Experts advise checking the attic first, since fixing it makes any later investment work more effectively.
options: Starting Home Energy Savings in the Attic
Replacing Old Windows with Double-Glazed Ones
Paying Back Costs Within a Few Winters
Reducing Household Energy Costs
quests.correctAnswer: Starting Home Energy Savings in the Attic
quests.hint: Which title reflects the advice about where to begin?
quests.explanation: Energy costs is too broad, windows are a foil, and the payback time is a supporting fact. The passage's recommendation is to start with attic insulation.
quests.whyThisTitle: This title names the step that the experts advise doing first.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: When a student asks for the answer, a good tutor often responds with a question. What have you tried? What does the problem tell you? At first, this frustrates students, who feel they are being kept from the solution. Over time, they begin asking themselves the same questions. Tutors say the goal is not to make students struggle but to move the thinking from the teacher's head into theirs.
options: Ways to Help Students Learn
Why Students Feel Frustrated
Asking Students What They Have Tried
Teaching by Asking Instead of Telling
quests.correctAnswer: Teaching by Asking Instead of Telling
quests.hint: The final sentence states the tutors' goal. What does it say?
quests.explanation: Ways to help students is broader, and asking what they have tried and their frustration are pieces of the method. The passage explains the method and its purpose.
quests.whyThisTitle: This choice states the method and, through the closing sentence, its aim of transferring the thinking.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: Chess engines now play far better than any human, yet human tournaments are more popular than ever. Top players use engines to test ideas and find hidden mistakes in their preparation. But spectators still come to see human decisions, made under pressure and sometimes wrong. Coaches say the engines have not replaced players; they have changed what players study, shifting attention from memorizing openings to understanding why moves work.
options: Artificial Intelligence and Games
Chess Engines Reshape How Players Train
Spectators Watching Humans Under Pressure
Testing Ideas for Hidden Mistakes
quests.correctAnswer: Chess Engines Reshape How Players Train
quests.hint: What have engines changed, and what have they left as it was?
quests.explanation: Artificial intelligence and games is too wide, and testing ideas and spectators each cover one part. The coaches' comment sums up the main change: how players study.
quests.whyThisTitle: The best title captures the change in training that the coaches describe.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In earthquake zones, engineers often build with flexibility rather than pure strength. A rigid building resists shaking until it cracks, whereas a flexible one sways and absorbs the energy. Some skyscrapers include huge weights or rubber bearings that move opposite to the shaking. Older buildings can be retrofitted with steel braces, though this costs money. The lesson from past disasters is that yielding a little can save a building.
options: The Cost of Retrofitting Old Buildings
Rubber Bearings Beneath Skyscrapers
Flexible Design That Protects Against Earthquakes
Preparing Cities for Natural Disasters
quests.correctAnswer: Flexible Design That Protects Against Earthquakes
quests.hint: Which sentence sums up the passage's lesson?
quests.explanation: Preparing cities is broader, and the bearings and retrofit costs are details. The passage explains why flexibility is the better approach.
quests.whyThisTitle: It states the principle the passage explains and illustrates.

quests.instruction: Drag the best title for the passage.
quests.passage: In some libraries, children who struggle with reading sit on a rug and read aloud to a therapy dog. The dog does not correct mistakes or hurry them. Teachers report that children read for longer, enjoy books more, and lose some of their fear of reading in public. Libraries that started with a single dog now have waiting lists for sessions. The animals' calm attention seems to matter more than any technique.
options: Animals in Education
A Calm Dog Builds Reading Confidence
Waiting Lists for Library Sessions
Teachers Noticing Longer Reading Sessions
quests.correctAnswer: A Calm Dog Builds Reading Confidence
quests.hint: Ask why the dogs help, not only that they do.
quests.explanation: Animals in education is far too broad, and the waiting lists and longer sessions are results. The main point is that the dog's non-judging presence helps children gain confidence.
quests.whyThisTitle: The title ties the dog's calm attention to the children's growing confidence.
